title: AI incidents of 2026: Rogue agents, stolen keys, and other familiar stories
content:
TL;DR
- We reviewed 50 AI-related security incidents from 2026 to understand how AI was involved and what actually went wrong.
- Most came back to familiar security problems: exposed credentials, excessive permissions, weak isolation and compromised vendors.
- AI helped attackers move faster, while agents introduced additional risks by acting beyond their intended boundaries.
- A lot of these incidents show how much familiar security practices still matter, especially as AI speeds things up.
- For exposed secrets and supply chain risk, Aikido Device Protection finds plaintext credentials on developer machines and blocks malicious installs, and Secrets detection catches API keys in code.
- For over-scoped access and weak isolation, Attack Path Analysis shows what a compromised workload could reach. AI Capabilities pentests check agents for actions they shouldn't take, and Zen blocks injection attacks at runtime.
Reading past the headline
It feels like every security incident we hear about lately has AI somewhere in it. But AI and the role it plays can mean a lot of different things. In some incidents, AI was the weakness an attacker exploited. In others, AI was the tool they attacked with. We wanted to understand which role AI played and what went wrong in each incident, because knowing the root cause tells us what to monitor, detect and fix going forward.
So we went through 50 incidents disclosed this year through November 19 and wrote down every root cause their reports stated. A lot of it came back to familiar problems, like exposed secrets, over-privileged accounts, weak isolation and compromised vendors. AI changed how some of these incidents played out, but the underlying failures weren’t always something new. Here’s what we found.
A few you’ve probably heard about
You’ve probably heard about most of these as “AI incidents.” Here are a few of them, with what each one came down to.
- Meta (April-May 2026). Attackers used an AI support assistant to initiate password resets for Instagram accounts they didn’t own. The recovery system failed to verify that the supplied email belonged to the account, potentially exposing up to 20,225 accounts.
- OpenAI and Hugging Face (July 2026). AI agents escaped their intended test boundaries and reached Hugging Face's platform. The sandbox could reach systems it shouldn't have, monitoring raised an alert but the run continued, and a shared long-lived admin credential gave the agents access to infrastructure beyond their intended scope.
- Online retailers (September 2026). AI agents ran a card skimming campaign across at least 27 retailers and took more than 600,000 cards from two of them. They got in through a SQL injection in a login field and then added skimmers to the checkout code without setting off any alerts.
- ConnectWise (October 2026). Storm-0940 used ARTEX, an agentic offensive framework, to attempt sign-ins against more than 2,250 tenants. ARTEX automated reconnaissance, authentication attempts, and actions such as modifying credentials and privileges. The attackers took advantage of compromised applications that already had trusted access to customer environments, allowing them to operate without users signing in.
- Railway (October 2026). An AI-assisted attacker exposed tokens for 1,852 users, and about $740,000 of unauthorized usage followed. The path there was customer builds sharing a VM, plus a build credential that worked on internal systems it was never meant for.
October alone accounted for seventeen of the 50 incidents we reviewed, of which nine involved AI development and hosting platforms. Some organizations published detailed reports explaining what went wrong, while others are still investigating or haven’t shared enough to identify a cause.
ARTEX and other agentic offensive frameworks appeared in several of the incidents we reviewed from October. These tools use AI agents to automate parts of an attack, from reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery to exploitation. The underlying techniques aren't particularly new, but these frameworks can explore different attack paths, adapt when something fails, and carry out attacks with far less human involvement.
AI’s different roles in cybersecurity incidents
Cybersecurity is still cybersecurity, but with some AI added to the mix. Sometimes AI was the target, sometimes it was the tool being used, and other times AI agents were deployed without enough guardrails.
- AI as the target. In 25 of the 50 incidents, attackers went after AI platforms, developer tools and services holding AI credentials. They targeted API keys, infrastructure and software packages, often with familiar techniques.
- AI as the attack tool. In 12 incidents, attackers used AI agents or agentic frameworks like ARTEX to carry out parts of the attack themselves. AI used to write malware or phishing lures isn’t counted here.
- AI without enough guardrails. In the other 13, AI agents running in products or test environments were set up with too few limits. Some followed instructions from untrusted sources, and others had permissions that let them reach systems or take actions no one meant them to.
This, however, doesn't tell us much about why they happened. For that, we looked at the underlying failures across all 50 incidents. And despite the different ways AI was involved, a lot of the same problems kept showing up.
Exposed secrets showed up more than anything else
Nothing near the top of that chart is exotic. We see secrets left where they could be found, tokens that could reach too far, trouble that came in through a vendor, and boundaries between systems that didn’t hold. Only 3 of the 50 incidents we reviewed involved a reported previously unknown vulnerability.
Even in those three, the unknown vulnerability only got the attacker in. What happened next depended on familiar controls. At Railway, an over-scoped build credential and a long-lived decryption key turned one escape into access to around 100,000 workspaces’ secrets. At Hugging Face, exposed tokens and a shared admin credential helped the agents spread to code running on 41 production servers. At DIVD, an AI agent chained two previously unknown flaws in its Zammad helpdesk to get root access, but network segmentation kept the damage mostly to volunteer contact details.
Most of these failure points are common, and we’d bet plenty of security teams could find at least one of them in their own environments today. In these 50 cases, someone else found the problem first. The organizations that shared what happened gave the rest of us something to learn from and a chance to fix the same weak spots in our own environments.
What AI did change is the pace and the prize. In one campaign Microsoft tracked, there were multiple cases where attackers using an agent framework went from first targeting to privileged access in under three hours. And with AI platforms, stolen credentials can quickly turn into unauthorized usage and significant costs.
The root causes
These problems often overlap. Take Vercel’s April incident. An employee connected a third-party AI tool to their corporate Google account, and the workspace settings allowed it broad permissions. When the tool’s vendor was compromised, the attacker got in through those existing permissions. The vendor compromise was the starting point, and the breadth of access the tool had been granted made the impact much worse.
We saw this pattern across most of the incidents: 35 of the 44 with a stated cause had more than one failure point. An exposed credential, broad permissions and limited monitoring can each be a problem on their own. Put them together, and an attacker has a much easier path through an environment.
This overlap matters when you think about prevention. Fixing one weakness might not stop an attack entirely, but it can limit how far an attacker gets. The same goes for agents running inside your own environment. Limiting what they can access, keeping credentials out

report.summary: A review of 50 AI-related security incidents from 2026 finds most failures were familiar ones — exposed secrets, over-privileged access, weak isolation — with AI mainly speeding attackers up.
report.background: Through 2026, AI agents moved from demos into production: coding assistants, support bots, browser agents and autonomous workflows, each wired into real systems with API keys, cloud roles and third-party OAuth grants. That created a new attack surface layered on top of old hygiene problems. Meanwhile, agentic offensive frameworks such as ARTEX began automating reconnaissance, credential stuffing and privilege changes, and AI development and hosting platforms became high-value targets because a single leaked token could unlock thousands of customer environments. Aikido reviewed 50 disclosed incidents through November 19, 2026, and recorded every stated root cause. The pattern: AI changed the tempo and the payoff of attacks far more than it changed the underlying weaknesses, which remain the same issues security teams have chased for a decade.
key_points: Only 3 of the 50 incidents involved a previously unknown vulnerability, and even there the flaw was just the entry point. What determined the damage was familiar control failure: over-scoped build credentials at Railway, shared admin credentials at Hugging Face, missing network segmentation at DIVD. Exotic AI-specific exploits were the exception, not the rule.

Exposed secrets topped the root-cause list. Long-lived API keys, tokens with far broader reach than needed, and plaintext credentials on developer machines repeatedly turned a small breach into a large one — Railway's single leaked build credential cascaded into roughly 100,000 workspaces' secrets and about $740,000 in unauthorized usage.

AI played three distinct roles: the target in 25 incidents (attackers hunting AI platforms, dev tools and model credentials), the attack tool in 12 (agentic frameworks automating recon and exploitation), and an unguarded actor in 13, where agents followed untrusted instructions or took actions nobody intended, as in the Meta password-reset abuse.

Failures compounded. Of the 44 incidents with a stated cause, 35 had more than one failure point — an exposed key plus broad permissions plus thin monitoring. Vercel's April case shows the chain: a compromised third-party AI tool inherited the wide Google Workspace access an employee had granted it.

Speed is what AI genuinely changed. Microsoft tracked agent-framework campaigns reaching privileged access from first targeting in under three hours, and October alone produced 17 of the 50 incidents, nine of them at AI development and hosting platforms.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the report argues that agent security is mostly conventional security applied rigorously: short-lived scoped credentials, least privilege for tool-using agents, real sandbox isolation, egress controls and monitoring that actually stops a run rather than just alerting. Vendors will face pressure to ship safe defaults and per-agent identity instead of shared admin keys. For developers, the practical risk is the integration sprawl around them — OAuth grants to third-party AI tools, secrets in build pipelines, and agents that can reach internal systems they were never meant to touch. For regular users, the fallout is measurable: mass password resets, hundreds of thousands of skimmed cards, stolen tokens billed to their accounts. The reassuring takeaway is that basic hygiene still breaks most attack chains.
report.tools: To follow up: Aikido's Secrets Detection, Device Protection, Attack Path Analysis, AI Capabilities pentesting and Zen runtime blocking address the report's four recurring failure modes. Open-source equivalents worth trying include Gitleaks and TruffleHog for secret scanning, Semgrep for code and config rules, Open Policy Agent for least-privilege enforcement, and gVisor or Firecracker for stronger agent sandboxing; pair them with the OWASP LLM and Agentic AI threat guidance.
